title: Niagara police investigate 'hate-motivated' vandalism in St. Catharines, Ont.
summary: Niagara police say they are investigating an act of vandalism Saturday in St. Catharines, Ont., as a "hate-motivated crime." B'nai Brith Canada says the incident is part of a disturbing trend of…

image.caption: Aleks Goldshtein said his Volkswagen car was badly vandalized after it was towed to a repair shop in St. Catharines, Ont. (Aleks Goldshtein photo)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Niagara police say they are investigating an act of vandalism Saturday in St. Catharines, Ont., as a "hate-motivated crime." B'nai Brith Canada says the incident is part of a disturbing trend of escalating antisemitism in Canada
B'nai Brith Canada says incident reflects growing antisemitism nationally
WARNING: This story includes a picture of a swastika.
Niagara police say they are investigating an act of vandalism Saturday in St. Catharines, Ont., as a "hate-motivated" crime.

They say a 2011 grey Volkswagen Passat on Oakdale Avenue was damaged, with its windows broken and hate symbols spray-painted on its side. The car is being examined by the police's forensic unit, they said in a news release.

The release also said that officers are reviewing a social media post relating to this incident and the "Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Unit has been made aware of the incident and will be engaged with the victim."
Aleks Goldshtein said it was his car that was badly vandalized in St. Catharines, though there was no confirmation from police.
Goldshtein, who is Jewish, said he's afraid for his own safety and the safety of his daughter because of the attack.
The human rights organization B'nai Brith Canada said the incident is part of a disturbing trend of escalating antisemitism in Canada.

Goldshtein, who said he is originally from Odesa, Ukraine, and who lived in Israel for five years at one point, sent photos of a grey Passat to CBC that he said is his car, with a swastika spray-painted on the side.

The swastika is widely associated with the Nazi Party of Germany, which among its atrocities during the Second World War committed the systemic murder of six million Jewish people during the Holocaust, along with millions of Roma, 2SLGBTQ+ and other victims.
Car found vandalized at repair shop
Niagara Regional Police said they launched their investigation on Saturday and the car was found vandalized while parked at an automotive repair shop on Oakdale Avenue.
Const. Jessica Martin, a spokesperson, said the police service cannot specify what symbols were spray-painted on the car because it doesn't wish to further spread the use of hate symbols.

On Tuesday, Goldshtein told CBC that his car broke down late at night on Oct. 29 and was towed to a parking lot at a service shop on Oakdale Avenue. He said he left a note in the window about the breakdown, noting he would arrange repairs.
The car had a small Israeli flag attached to the inside of the windshield, he said.

Goldshtein said someone called him the next day to report someone damaging his car. When he went to see it, he saw the extensive damage and the swastika spray-painted on the side. The flag was repositioned into a small hole in the windshield, he said.
Goldshtein said he relied on the car for income, to make deliveries.

Goldshtein says he had this small Israeli flag inside his windshield when it was towed to a repair shop in St. Catharines after a vehicle breakdown. The flag was stuck in a hole in the damaged windshield. (Aleks Goldshtein photo)
He said he's particularly worried because the person or persons who carried out the vandalism may have learned where he lives by ransacking the interior.
"Documents containing my personal information were inside the vehicle, including documents showing my full name, home address and phone number," he said.

"Considering the seriousness of what happened, the exposure of my personal information and the fact that police are now officially investigating the incident as hate-motivated, I believe it is reasonable for me to take my family’s safety very seriously," he said.
"My greatest concern is my daughter. Her safety comes first for me."

blocks.text: Goldshtein said that after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Russia, his family spent time in Europe, including Germany, before arriving in Canada in 2023 under the Canada–Ukraine Authorization for Emergency Travel program.
"Canada and the Niagara Region became the place where we tried to rebuild our lives," he said.
Hoping for help to keep safe
Asked by CBC News if he feels less safe in Niagara now, Goldshtein, who didn't want to name the city he lives in, said his sense of safety has been compromised.

"I do not believe that St. Catharines as a community is unsafe, and I have received a great deal of kindness and support from people in Niagara," he said. "[But] what makes me feel unsafe is that I do not know who ultimately committed all of the damage or what information they may now have about me."
He said one of his most urgent needs now is safe and confidential temporary housing, ideally a place where his location would not be publicly known.
"I am willing to relocate to another city or even another province if necessary while the investigation continues."
He hopes victim support programs, Jewish community organizations or other organizations may help him.
Richard Robertson, director of research and advocacy for B'nai Brith Canada, told CBC News on Tuesday that the incident in St. Catharines is not an isolated one.
"It is part of a national crisis of antisemitism. This really is an assault on our nation and its values."
Large rise in antisemitic cases

Robertson said there was a 140 per cent increase in the number of antisemitic incidents between 2022 and 2025, and a 220 per cent increase in the number of violent incidents of antisemitism already in 2026 compared to all of last year

"[It] is not only an affront to the Jewish community; it is contradictory to Canadian values and to the Canada which we all know and love," he said. "That a vehicle could not even be left alone overnight, with an Israeli flag in the vehicle, without the vehicle subsequently being vandalized with hateful antisemitic graffiti, is an appalling testament to the state of hate in this country.

blocks.text: "This incident is just yet another disgusting example of how normalized anti-Semitism has become in Canada in 2026."
Niagara police are asking anyone with information about the vandalism to contact them.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Paul Forsyth is a St. Catharines-based CBC reporter covering communities in the Niagara Region. He has decades of reporting experience in Niagara, having worked for Niagara This Week, the St. Catharines Standard and the Welland Tribune before joining CBC. You can reach him at paul.forsyth@cbc.ca.
